title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators (an execution validator and a graph-based static reachability analyzer) combined by logical OR, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms (model_calls_used = 300). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was never invoked, the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs; instead it quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the verifier predicate under the chosen contract. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) is increasingly attractive, but operators worry that generated configurations may expand attack surface or violate policy. Prior work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. However, evidence that placing a formal verifier inside a GVR loop meaningfully reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs remains limited and often informal.

This study asks a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? We designed and preregistered a deterministic paired experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and executed it under a frozen adapter contract that traded provider calls for deterministic accounting. Our concrete, evidence-supported contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired N = 300 confirmatory design with deterministic emulation and two validators combined by logical OR; (2) deterministic execution and provider-call accounting under a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM output replayed to both arms), with complete per-episode validator traces archived; (3) a transparent confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300, no discordant pairs) together with exact statistical summaries (McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap CI [0.0,0.0], Clopper–Pearson bound ≈0.00994) and an explicit statement that the preregistered repair-efficacy hypothesis was untestable in this run; and (4) artifact-grounded design recommendations for follow-up stress tests that can exercise repair paths (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, larger repair budgets, and more diverse verifiers).
sections.related_work: Three strands of verified literature motivated our work. First, execution-guided generate–verify–repair systems for code and infrastructure (e.g., TerraFormer) show that verifier feedback can improve correctness when the verifier and repair strategy are appropriate. Second, surveys and NetOps systems work document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and emphasize validators, constraints, or human oversight to reduce risk. Third, emulation and testbed research demonstrates practical execution-based validation but warns about external-validity gaps between controlled emulators and production networks. Our study differs by providing a preregistered paired confirmatory design with deterministic validator traces and explicit generation-semantics accounting to study whether inserting a verifier changes observed compliance under a concrete adapter contract.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) fixed a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents producing forbidden reachability), tested via an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). CIs were prespecified via bootstrap percentile; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) as recorded in the analysis log.

Task generation and emulation: Intent tasks were programmatically generated from public NetOps task corpora and synthetic perturbations; exact generation seeds, per-task payloads, and emulator composition (Dockerized FRRouting-style container images) are archived in the execution manifest and task manifest. Execution determinism was enforced through containerized validators and seeded generators; the run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed episodes = 600 and failed episodes = 0.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit provider calls the preregistered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent a single initial LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms. This choice causes baseline to be a replayed sample rather than an independent LLM draw; model_calls_used = 300 under this contract (maximum_model_calls allowed by the contract = 600). The provider-call audit records the stage 'shared_initial_generation' = 300.

Intervention (Guarded) and baseline: Baseline = shared initial candidate replayed directly. Guarded = same candidate validated by deterministic validators; a repair LLM call was permitted (max one repair per pair) only if any validator detected forbidden reachability. The repair prompt template and invocation rule were preregistered and are archived in the transformation manifest. Across the run no repair calls were issued because validators never reported forbidden reachability.

Forbidden-reachability predicate and validators (concise technical definition): The forbidden-reachability predicate used in scoring flags any final configuration that—when evaluated by the validators—permits an end-to-end forwarding reachability (under the emulated forwarding/routing semantics) from a protected origin to a destination explicitly marked by the task as forbidden (e.g., escalation of access from a protected management interface to a restricted service endpoint). This predicate covers both data-plane forwarding and control-plane route acceptance as represented in the emulator and task policy annotations. Two deterministic validators implemented complementary checks: (1) an execution-style validator (Batfish-like, containerized) that parses CLI, applies it in the FRRouting-style emulation image, and tests concrete reachability queries under the emulated forwarding plane; and (2) a graph-based static reachability analyzer implemented in Python that computes abstract forwarding graphs and applies policy predicates. The two validators were combined with a logical OR: any validator indicating forbidden reachability labels the episode as violating. Per-episode validator outputs, the validator_id ('deterministic_netops_validator_v5') and validator_version ('5.0'), and the decision rule are archived in the scoring artifacts for full inspection.

Analysis plan and sensitivity: Primary analysis used McNemar exact test on complete matched pairs; prespecified sensitivity analyses would treat technical or model failures as violations. No technical/model failures occurred. All raw responses, per-episode validator traces, and provider-call audits are archived and cited as reproducibility evidence.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed all planned episodes (600) without failures. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract shows model_calls_used = 300 (one generation per pair). The execution manifest records start and end times and the provider-call stage 'shared_initial_generation' = 300.

Primary confirmatory outcome: All 300 complete pairs were compliant in both arms with respect to the forbidden-reachability predicate: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The exact McNemar two-sided p-value = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.0, 0.0].

Descriptive bound on undetected baseline violations: Observing 0/300 baseline violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the (unknown) baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). We report this numeric upper bound as the proper descriptive inference available from the data: under the exact contract and validators used, the baseline violation rate is bounded above by ≈0.00994 with 95% confidence.

Repair activity and verifier concordance: No validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; consequently no repair call was invoked (per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false across archived scoring artifacts). The two validators were concordant on all episodes (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in archived analysis artifacts). Representative task artifacts (shared-initial / baseline / guarded response files and scoring JSON) illustrate typical normalized configurations and validator traces; examples are archived for spot-checking.

Statistical interpretation: The confirmatory McNemar test is uninformative for the preregistered repair-efficacy hypothesis because it requires discordant pairs (n10 or n01 > 0) to compare paired outcomes. The observed degenerate contingency (n11 = 300 only) results from two coupled design facts: (a) the shared_initial_candidate contract reduces between-arm sampling variance (baseline is a replayed sample), and (b) the sampled adversarial variants did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. Therefore the experiment answers a different, artifact-grounded question: under the chosen model, validators, emulator, adversary generator, and shared-generation contract, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on the sampled intents, and inserting the verifier did not change this observed compliance.
sections.discussion:
What the data support: The archived artifacts (provider-call audit, per-episode validator traces, contingency table and analysis logs) unambiguously show that, under the exact adapter contract and validator set, baseline outputs already met the forbidden-reachability safety predicate on all sampled intents; therefore inserting a verifier did not alter observed compliance. The one-sided Clopper–Pearson bound quantifies the maximum baseline violation rate consistent with observing 0/300 violations (≈0.00994 at 95% confidence).

What the data do not support: Because the repair path was never triggered, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and sought to detect a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the degenerate observed contingency violates that assumption and renders the primary confirmatory test moot for repair efficacy.

Design lessons (artifact-grounded recommendations): (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces provider calls but also reduces independent-sample variance needed to observe discordant violating outputs. For experiments intended to exercise repair efficacy, use independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or increase the repair-call budget. The execution manifest records the cost trade-off (model_calls_used = 300 vs up to 600 under independent draws). (2) Adversary potency matters: deterministic programmatic adversarial variants used here did not elicit verifier-detectable violations; stronger, targeted adversaries are required to exercise repair. (3) Verifier diversity and strength matter: testing multiple oracle families, including production-grade execution oracles, increases the chance of detecting violations and exercising repair logic. (4) Reproducible accounting is practical: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, and provider-call audits archived here permit exact replay of the deterministic accounting and statistical summaries.

Threats to validity (artifact-located): Internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json). Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators sufficiently capture operational security risk; validator capabilities and limitations are documented per episode in scoring artifacts. External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and run in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions are unmet. All referenced artifacts are archived to support independent reanalysis and targeted follow-up runs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration using a declared LLM (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, no repair path was exercised and the experiment cannot evaluate verifier-guided repair efficacy. The primary, artifact-supported takeaways are operational: (a) generation semantics, adversary design, and verifier strength materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations; (b) deterministic, per-episode artifact archiving enables precise accounting and reproducible bounds on undetected violation rates; and (c) follow-up stress tests should (i) use independent-condition generation or larger model-call budgets, (ii) craft stronger adversaries targeting verifier predicates, and (iii) evaluate multiple models and richer verifier families to exercise repair paths. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts in the evidence bundle to enable reproducible follow-up studies and targeted stress tests that can evaluate repair efficacy directly.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
